title: Formal Charges and Resonance
lead: When more than one Lewis structure can be written for a molecule or ion, formal charges help us decide which is the most reasonable. Some molecules and ions are described by no single Lewis structure, and resonance describes them by several at once.
objectives: Compute formal charges for atoms in any Lewis structure
Use formal charges to identify the most reasonable Lewis structure for a given molecule
Explain the concept of resonance and draw Lewis structures representing resonance forms for a given molecule
summary_html: In a Lewis structure, formal charges can be assigned to each atom by treating each bond as if one-half of the electrons are assigned to each atom. These hypothetical formal charges are a guide to determining the most appropriate Lewis structure. A structure in which the formal charges are as close to zero as possible is preferred. Resonance occurs in cases where two or more Lewis structures with identical arrangements of atoms but different distributions of electrons can be written. The actual distribution of electrons (the resonance hybrid) is an average of the distribution indicated by the individual Lewis structures (the resonance forms).

exercises.prompt:
Write resonance forms that describe the distribution of electrons in each of these molecules or ions.
(a) selenium dioxide, OSeO
(b) nitrate ion, ${\text{NO}}_{3}{}^{\text{−}}$
(c) nitric acid, HNO3 (N is bonded to an OH group and two O atoms)
(d) benzene, C6H6:

(e) the formate ion:

answer.solution:
In each case one double bond can be drawn to any of two or three equivalent atoms, and the forms are joined by double-headed arrows.
(a) OSeO, 6 + 2(6) = 18 electrons, has two forms, O=Se–O ↔ O–Se=O. Selenium carries one lone pair, the double-bonded oxygen two lone pairs and the single-bonded oxygen three.
(b) ${\text{NO}}_{3}{}^{\text{−}}$, 5 + 3(6) + 1 = 24 electrons, has three forms, like carbonate. Nitrogen has one N=O and two N–O bonds and no lone pair; the double-bonded oxygen carries two lone pairs and each single-bonded oxygen three, and the double bond goes to each oxygen in turn.
(c) HNO3, 24 electrons, has two forms. The OH oxygen is single bonded to N and carries two lone pairs, and the double bond goes to either of the two other oxygen atoms, which then carry two and three lone pairs.
(d) C6H6, 6(4) + 6(1) = 30 electrons, has two forms. Single and double bonds alternate around the ring, three C=C bonds in all, and in the second form every double bond has moved one position around the ring.
(e) The formate ion, 4 + 2(6) + 1 + 1 = 18 electrons, has two forms. Carbon is bonded to H, double bonded to one oxygen, which carries two lone pairs, and single bonded to the other, which carries three; the double bond may go to either oxygen. Both forms are in brackets with charge –.

exercises.prompt: Write the resonance forms of ozone, O<sub>3</sub>, the component of the upper atmosphere that protects the Earth from ultraviolet radiation.

answer.solution: Ozone has two resonance forms, O=O–O ↔ O–O=O. The three oxygen atoms have 3(6) = 18 valence electrons. In each form the central oxygen atom has one double bond, one single bond and one lone pair; the double-bonded terminal oxygen carries two lone pairs and the single-bonded one carries three, so every atom has an octet. The central atom reaches its octet only if one of its bonds is a double bond, and the two terminal atoms are equivalent, so the double bond may be drawn to either one. The forms are joined by a double-headed arrow, as for the nitrite ion. The resonance hybrid has two identical O–O bonds, each the average of a single and a double bond.

exercises.prompt: Sodium nitrite, which has been used to preserve bacon and other meats, is an ionic compound. Write the resonance forms of the nitrite ion, ${\text{NO}}_{\text{2}}{}^{\text{–}}\text{.}$

In terms of the bonds present, explain why acetic acid, CH3CO2H, contains two distinct types of carbon-oxygen bonds, whereas the acetate ion, formed by loss of a hydrogen ion from acetic acid, only contains one type of carbon-oxygen bond. The skeleton structures of these species are shown:

answer.solution: Acetic acid has one C=O double bond and one C–O single bond, while in the acetate ion both carbon-oxygen bonds are the same, each the average of a single and a double bond. In acetic acid, the second carbon atom reaches an octet only with a double bond to one oxygen. The oxygen atom that carries the hydrogen atom already has two bonds and two lone pairs, so the double bond goes to the other oxygen, and only one Lewis structure can be written: a shorter C=O bond and a longer C–O bond. When the hydrogen ion leaves, the two oxygen atoms are bonded alike, and the double bond may be drawn to either of them, giving two resonance forms with the negative charge on the single-bonded oxygen. The acetate ion is the resonance hybrid of those forms, so its two C–O bonds are identical, as the two N–O bonds of nitrite are.

exercises.prompt: Toothpastes containing sodium hydrogen carbonate (sodium bicarbonate) and hydrogen peroxide are widely used. Write Lewis structures for the hydrogen carbonate ion and hydrogen peroxide molecule, with resonance forms where appropriate.

answer.solution: The hydrogen carbonate ion, ${\text{HCO}}_{3}{}^{\text{−}}$, has two resonance forms, and hydrogen peroxide has one Lewis structure and no resonance forms. ${\text{HCO}}_{3}{}^{\text{−}}$ has 1 + 4 + 3(6) + 1 = 24 valence electrons. Carbon is bonded to an OH group, whose oxygen carries two lone pairs, and to two other oxygen atoms, one by a double bond, with two lone pairs on that oxygen, and one by a single bond, with three lone pairs; the structure is in brackets with charge –. The double bond may go to either of the two oxygen atoms without hydrogen, so the two forms are joined by a double-headed arrow. Hydrogen peroxide has 2(1) + 2(6) = 14 valence electrons: H–O–O–H, with two lone pairs on each oxygen. Every atom is complete with single bonds alone, and no other placement of the electrons keeps the same arrangement of atoms, so H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> has no resonance forms.

exercises.prompt:
Determine the formal charge of each element in the following:
(a) HCl
(b) CF4
(c) PCl3
(d) PF5

Determine the formal charge of each element in the following:
(a) H3O+
(b) ${\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}$
(c) NH3
(d) ${\text{O}}_{2}{}^{\text{2−}}$
(e) H2O2

answer.solution:
Each formal charge is the valence electrons of the free atom, less the lone pair electrons, less half of the bonding electrons.
(a) H3O+: O, +1; H, 0. Oxygen has three bonds and one lone pair, 6 – 2 – 3 = +1, and each H is 1 – 0 – 1 = 0. The sum, +1, is the charge of the ion.
(b) ${\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}$: S, +2; O, –1. In the structure with four S–O single bonds and three lone pairs on each oxygen, sulfur is 6 – 0 – 4 = +2 and each oxygen 6 – 6 – 1 = –1, and the sum is +2 + 4(–1) = –2.
(c) NH3: N, 0; H, 0. Nitrogen has three bonds and one lone pair, 5 – 2 – 3 = 0.
(d) ${\text{O}}_{2}{}^{\text{2−}}$: O, –1 each. The ion has 14 electrons, an O–O single bond and three lone pairs on each oxygen, 6 – 6 – 1 = –1, and the sum is –2.
(e) H2O2: O, 0; H, 0. In H–O–O–H each oxygen has two bonds and two lone pairs, 6 – 4 – 2 = 0, and the sum is zero, as it must be for a neutral molecule.

exercises.prompt:
Calculate the formal charge of each element in the following compounds and ions:
(a) F2CO
(b) NO–
(c) ${\text{BF}}_{4}{}^{\text{−}}$
(d) ${\text{SnCl}}_{3}{}^{\text{−}}$
(e) H2CCH2
(f) ClF3
(g) SeF6
(h) ${\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{\text{3−}}$

answer.solution:
Each formal charge is the valence electrons of the free atom, less the lone pair electrons, less half of the bonding electrons, and the charges of each species add up to its overall charge.
(a) F2CO: C, 0; O, 0; F, 0. Carbon has a C=O double bond and two C–F bonds, 4 – 0 – 4 = 0; oxygen, with two lone pairs, is 6 – 4 – 2 = 0; each F is 7 – 6 – 1 = 0.
(b) NO–: N, –1; O, 0. In N=O with two lone pairs on each atom, N is 5 – 4 – 2 = –1 and O is 6 – 4 – 2 = 0.
(c) ${\text{BF}}_{4}{}^{\text{−}}$: B, –1; F, 0. Boron has four single bonds, 3 – 0 – 4 = –1.
(d) ${\text{SnCl}}_{3}{}^{\text{−}}$: Sn, –1; Cl, 0. The 26 electrons give tin three single bonds and one lone pair, 4 – 2 – 3 = –1.
(e) H2CCH2: C, 0; H, 0. Each carbon has a double bond and two single bonds, 4 – 0 – 4 = 0.
(f) ClF3: Cl, 0; F, 0. Chlorine has three bonds and two lone pairs, 7 – 4 – 3 = 0.
(g) SeF6: Se, 0; F, 0. Selenium has six bonds and no lone pair, 6 – 0 – 6 = 0.
(h) ${\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{\text{3−}}$: P, +1; O, –1. Phosphorus has four single bonds, 5 – 0 – 4 = +1, and each oxygen, with three lone pairs, 6 – 6 – 1 = –1; the sum is +1 + 4(–1) = –3.

exercises.prompt: Based on formal charge considerations, which of the following would likely be the correct arrangement of atoms in nitrosyl chloride: ClNO or ClON?

answer.solution: ClNO is the likely arrangement. Both have 7 + 5 + 6 = 18 valence electrons. In ClNO, written Cl–N=O with three lone pairs on Cl, one on N and two on O, the formal charges are Cl 7 – 6 – 1 = 0, N 5 – 2 – 3 = 0 and O 6 – 4 – 2 = 0. In ClON, written Cl–O=N with three lone pairs on Cl, one on O and two on N, they are Cl 0, O 6 – 2 – 3 = +1 and N 5 – 4 – 2 = –1. A structure with all formal charges zero is preferable (Guideline 1), and ClON is worse still because it puts the negative formal charge on nitrogen rather than on the more electronegative oxygen (Guideline 4).

exercises.prompt: Based on formal charge considerations, which of the following would likely be the correct arrangement of atoms in sulfur dioxide: OSO or SOO?

answer.solution: OSO is the likely arrangement. Both have 3(6) = 18 valence electrons. In OSO, written O=S–O with one lone pair on S, the formal charges are S 6 – 2 – 3 = +1, double-bonded O 6 – 4 – 2 = 0 and single-bonded O 6 – 6 – 1 = –1. Sulfur is a third-period atom and may hold more than eight electrons, so O=S=O, with one lone pair on S, can also be written, and then every formal charge is zero: S 6 – 2 – 4 = 0 and each O 6 – 4 – 2 = 0. In SOO, written S=O–O with two lone pairs on S, one on the central O and three on the terminal O, the charges are S 0, central O 6 – 2 – 3 = +1 and terminal O –1; the central oxygen cannot exceed an octet, so no SOO structure has all zero formal charges, and every one puts a positive formal charge on an oxygen atom. OSO is preferred by Guideline 1, and it places the less electronegative atom, sulfur, in the center, as in carbon dioxide.

exercises.prompt:
Iodine forms a series of fluorides (listed here). Write Lewis structures for each of the four compounds and determine the formal charge of the iodine atom in each molecule:
(a) IF
(b) IF3
(c) IF5
(d) IF7

answer.solution:
The formal charge of iodine is 0 in all four compounds. Each fluorine atom forms one single bond to iodine and carries three lone pairs, 7 – 6 – 1 = 0, and the electrons left over go on iodine as lone pairs.
(a) IF, 7 + 7 = 14 electrons: I–F with three lone pairs on iodine; I is 7 – 6 – 1 = 0.
(b) IF3, 7 + 3(7) = 28 electrons: three I–F bonds and two lone pairs on iodine; I is 7 – 4 – 3 = 0.
(c) IF5, 7 + 5(7) = 42 electrons: five I–F bonds and one lone pair on iodine; I is 7 – 2 – 5 = 0.
(d) IF7, 7 + 7(7) = 56 electrons: seven I–F bonds and no lone pair on iodine; I is 7 – 0 – 7 = 0.
Iodine is hypervalent in IF3, IF5 and IF7, with 10, 12 and 14 electrons, which an atom of the fifth period can hold.

exercises.prompt: Which of the following structures would we expect for nitrous acid? Determine the formal charges:

answer.solution: The right-hand structure, H–O–N=O, is the expected one, because all its formal charges are zero. Formal charge is the valence electrons of the free atom, less the lone pair electrons, less half of the bonding electrons. In the left-hand structure, with hydrogen on nitrogen, nitrogen has four bonds and no lone pair, 5 – 0 – 4 = +1; the single-bonded oxygen, with three lone pairs, is 6 – 6 – 1 = –1; the double-bonded oxygen is 6 – 4 – 2 = 0; and H is 0. In the right-hand structure, H is 0; the oxygen bonded to hydrogen, with two bonds and two lone pairs, is 6 – 4 – 2 = 0; nitrogen, with three bonds and one lone pair, is 5 – 2 – 3 = 0; and the terminal oxygen is 6 – 4 – 2 = 0. Both sets add up to zero, but a structure in which all formal charges are zero is preferable (Guideline 1).
